titre: The Dead Sea Scrolls: Who Copied Them, and Where?
accroche: They are said to have been written by the Essenes of Qumran. The identification rests on a passage in Pliny and on a reading of the ruins that others dispute.
contenu_vulgarise:
Almost every article on the Dead Sea Scrolls attributes them to the Essenes of Qumran, a community of ascetics who supposedly copied the scrolls in their “scriptorium” before hiding them in eleven caves. The whole picture rests on a hypothesis that scholars continue to debate, and every element that supports it has been challenged.

## What Was Actually Found

Between November 1946 and February 1947, Bedouin shepherds discovered the first scrolls in caves near Qumran, on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea. Excavations of the caves continued until 1956: in all, about 981 manuscripts came out of eleven caves. About four in ten are biblical books, including the Great Isaiah Scroll, and only one book is missing: Esther. The rest mixes non-canonical Jewish texts with writings that set out the rules of a particular group.

The Essene hypothesis comes from an ancient text. Pliny the Elder, in his *Natural History* (V, 73), places a tribe of Essenes, without women and without money, on the west bank of the Dead Sea, living above En Gedi. Roland de Vaux, who excavated the site of Khirbet Qumran from 1951 to 1956, linked this passage to the nearby ruins, saw a monastery there, and called one room a “scriptorium” because of the inkwells found in it.

## What Remains Disputed

The neighboring cemetery has about 1,100 graves according to de Vaux, mostly of men but also a few women (some of the graves may, however, be medieval): this fits poorly with a community without women. Other readings of the site have been proposed: a Hasmonean fortress, a wealthy agricultural villa, a pottery-making center. Yitzhak Magen and Yuval Peleg argue that the site was converted into a pottery factory. Norman Golb, of the University of Chicago, argues in *Who Wrote the Dead Sea Scrolls?* (1995) that the scrolls are not the product of the Essenes but of many Jewish currents and communities; he would later develop a Jerusalem origin, with the manuscripts coming from Jerusalem libraries put in safekeeping before the Roman siege. Others propose a dissident Sadducean group, or an Essene group with Sadducean roots.

The Essene hypothesis remains the most widespread, but scholars do not agree.

## What This Changes

The manuscripts themselves are not in question: their date, from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE, rests on paleography and carbon-14. What is uncertain is the hand that copied them. A collection hidden in caves was not necessarily written where it was found.

repere.texte: Between 1946 and 1956, about 981 manuscripts were recovered from eleven caves near Qumran. Nearly four in ten are biblical books; a single book of the Hebrew Bible is missing from the collection, Esther.

carte.punch: The Dead Sea Scrolls are authentic. Who copied them is debated.
carte.idee: About 981 manuscripts, taken from eleven caves, dated from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE. Who copied them? The hypothesis of the Essenes of Qumran rests on Pliny and on de Vaux, but others see the work of many Jewish currents.

quiz.question: What makes the hypothesis that the Essenes of Qumran wrote the manuscripts debatable?
choix: The cemetery includes women, and the site can also be read as a fortress or a workshop
The manuscripts themselves would be modern forgeries, manufactured in the 20th century
Pliny the Elder mentions no community in this region: the hypothesis has no ancient basis
The language the manuscripts are written in has never been identified with certainty
quiz.explication: A cemetery that includes women and competing readings of the site (fortress, villa, pottery) weaken the Essene hypothesis. The manuscripts themselves are not in question: their antiquity is established by paleography and carbon-14. Pliny the Elder does describe a tribe of Essenes above En Gedi; that very passage is what founds the hypothesis. And the language of the manuscripts is known: mostly Hebrew, with some Aramaic and Greek.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which biblical book is missing among the Dead Sea Scrolls?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Book of Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible absent from the collection.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What thesis does Norman Golb defend in Who Wrote the Dead Sea Scrolls? (1995)?
choix: The scrolls were fabricated in the Middle Ages
The scrolls are the exclusive work of the Essenes
The scrolls are the product of many Jewish currents, not of the Essenes alone
The scrolls were imported from Rome
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Golb argues that the scrolls are not the product of the Essenes but of many Jewish currents and communities.
